title: AIPAC's Record $30 Million Bet on Michigan Faces Democratic Voter Revolt
excerpt: The pro-Israel lobby's largest-ever single-race investment has become a lightning rod in Michigan's Senate primary, as progressive challenger Abdul El-Sayed frames the spending as proof of a rigged political system.
body:
• AIPAC and allied groups have spent close to $50 million backing Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Aug. 4 Democratic Senate primary — their largest single-race investment ever
  • Progressive challenger Abdul El-Sayed has made the lobby's spending a centerpiece of his campaign, framing it as evidence of a political system captured by billionaire donors
  • A Quinnipiac poll found 66% of Democrats now believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 20% in 2017, signalling a generational shift in the party

Michigan's Democratic Senate primary on August 4 has become ground zero for the most expensive and ideologically charged intra-party battle over US-Israel policy in a generation. At the heart of it: nearly $30 million spent by AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and its super PAC United Democracy Project to elect Rep. Haley Stevens — and defeat progressive Abdul El-Sayed.

The spending is AIPAC's largest investment in a single race, ever. And it has turned the lobby itself into a central campaign issue, the Associated Press reported.

Context

Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, has largely avoided discussing AIPAC directly. During a July campaign stop in West Michigan, she responded to two questions about the group with more than 800 words — without mentioning it once, according to the AP. She has described herself as a "proud pro-Israel Democrat" and made a video with AIPAC arguing that a close relationship with Israel "yields trade, that yields economic growth and that keeps our freedoms safe."

https://x.com/OurRevolution/status/2083955793745871231

El-Sayed, a former public health official and the son of Egyptian immigrants, has taken the opposite approach. He calls Israel's military campaign in Gaza a "genocide," describes the Israeli government as "evil," and has made AIPAC's spending the defining issue of his campaign.

"She is nothing more than an employee of these billionaires."

— Sen. Bernie Sanders, campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan

Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have both rallied with El-Sayed across the state. His campaign says it has recruited over 10,000 volunteers, compared to "hundreds" reported by Stevens' team. But outside groups backing Stevens have spent close to $50 million — most of it on ads that never mention Israel, instead highlighting her work on manufacturing and featuring former President Barack Obama, the AP noted.

Impact

The Michigan race is not an isolated flashpoint. It sits atop a wave of anti-AIPAC energy that has reshaped Democratic primaries across the country in 2026. Two anti-AIPAC groups — Track AIPAC and Justice Democrats — have endorsed more than 100 Democratic candidates who pledged to reject pro-Israel donations, Reuters reported.

Progressive candidates critical of Israel have won House primaries in New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Colorado this cycle. In Colorado, Ethiopian-born Melat Kiros defeated longtime Rep. Diana DeGette on a platform calling for an end to military aid to Israel.

The shift is visible in Congress too. This month, 103 House Democrats voted to block $3.3 billion in US aid to Israel — a move that would have been unimaginable even two years ago. Among the yes votes: former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark.

"This is an unbelievably fast shift. We are witnessing in real time a total remake of the politics of the Israel relationship."

— Jeremy Ben-Ami, president of J Street

Public opinion data underscores the scale of the change. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of all voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel — up from 16% and 20% respectively when the question was first asked in 2017. Gallup data shows favorable views of Israel among Americans have dropped from 75% in 2021 to 46% in 2026.

The Diaspora Dimension

Michigan is home to the largest Arab American population in the United States, making the Israel question intensely personal for many voters. But the race also resonates with South Asian American communities watching how ethnic and religious identity shapes US electoral politics. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim US senator — a milestone with significance for minority communities navigating representation in American public life.

The broader question of foreign policy lobbying and its outsized role in US elections is one that Indian American political organisations have tracked closely, particularly as the diaspora's own political engagement deepens.

What's Next

The Aug. 4 primary will be a decisive test. Michigan political strategist Adrian Hemond told the AP that Stevens holds the structural advantage: "Seniors and Black voters in a statewide Democratic primary are two of your most reliable voting demographics." El-Sayed needs younger, less reliable primary voters to turn out in force.

Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Stevens late last week, a significant boost. But the outcome will reverberate far beyond Michigan. A victory for El-Sayed would be the most consequential win yet for an Israel critic in a competitive November race, CNN noted. Even a Stevens win, however, will not silence the backlash — not when half of House Democrats have already voted to cut off aid entirely.

The winner faces Republican Mike Rogers, who is unopposed in his primary, in November.
nri_angle: The Michigan race resonates with Indian American communities tracking how ethnic identity and foreign policy lobbying shape US elections, as the diaspora's own political engagement deepens.
